Chapter 6: Practices for Settling the Body
There’s a quiet strength in learning how to settle your body, especially when the world feels so unpredictable. You know, most of us have that first instinct—to just push through discomfort. Maybe you ignore a racing heart or that tight feeling in your chest. But here’s the thing: your body keeps track. If you keep brushing those signals aside, they stack up, and after a while, it gets harder to truly feel safe or at ease.
Let me share a story. There was a teacher who, after a long day wrangling restless students, would come home feeling totally drained and snappy. She started to notice her jaw was aching, and her shoulders felt like stone. One evening, instead of sinking into the couch and zoning out in front of the TV, she tried something different. She sat quietly, closed her eyes, and placed her hand over her heart. She took slow, gentle breaths, paying attention to her chest rising and falling. At first, her mind was racing with worries, but as she kept breathing, her body slowly began to soften. The tension eased—just a little. It wasn’t magic, but it was a beginning.
Most people don’t realize just how much their bodies crave this kind of care. Simple practices—like deep breathing, humming, or even gentle rocking—send a message to your nervous system: it’s okay to relax. These aren’t just relaxation tricks. They’re ways of teaching your body that it doesn’t always have to stay on high alert.
For folks carrying racialized trauma, though, settling the body might feel odd, or even uncomfortable. The body can resist, holding tight to old patterns of staying vigilant. But with patience, and by repeating these practices, something slowly shifts. Imagine a parent, after years of bracing for the worst, learning to pause before reacting to a child’s outburst. Or a police officer, always scanning for threats, deciding to ground themselves with slow, steady breaths before stepping out of their car. These small choices—these moments of settling—don’t erase the past, but they open up space for something new.
What becomes clear is that healing isn’t about forcing your body to relax. It’s about gently inviting it to feel safe—one breath, one moment at a time. And over weeks or months, these moments build up. They shift your baseline, from constant tension to something softer, something more at ease. The world might not change overnight, but the way your body meets the world absolutely can.
